title: Argosy Health - Escalation Postmortem Follow-up
summary: Follow-up on the 2027-11-17 production incident where Argosy observed elevated 5xx rates and tail latency during peak traffic. Reviewed root cause hypotheses (KV cache eviction + autoscaler misconfiguration), mitigations applied (rollback to stable model variant, temporary increase of dedicated capacity), and next steps for reliability hardening and runbook updates.
next_steps: Redwood to share full latency/error traces and aggregated KV cache stats by 2027-11-22
Argosy SRE and Redwood SE to run coordinated load test on staging (simulating 2x peak) week of 2027-11-29
Marcus to propose autoscaler tuning and a permanent dedicated capacity plan by 2027-11-24
Sofia to send updated pricing/commit options for Dedicated buffer within 48 hours
Lena to schedule a follow-up review 2 weeks after tests (target 2027-12-06)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-20
Time: 10:30 PT
Duration: ~55m
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Lena (CSM) — Daniel (Argosy VP Eng), Priya (Argosy SRE), Tom (CTO)

[00:00] Sofia Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is the follow-up for the escalation, we want to make sure we captured the root cause and next steps, um Marcus will run through the instrumentation we collected
[00:18] Marcus Liu: yeah hi, uh so quick recap, on 11/17 around 14:05 UTC Argosy saw a spike in 5xxs and tail latency — requests that previously sat at ~120ms p95 spiked to p99s in the multiple seconds, concurrent errors around 0.8-1.2% of traffic at the worst window
[00:36] Priya Nair: yep that's what we saw, and it coincided with a product batch job that increased fanout to recommendation endpoints, note that fanout was roughly 2.1x our normal peak
[00:50] Marcus Liu: right and from our traces the sequence was: model variant rollout started, some requests hit a new quantized variant which has a slightly different KV-cache footprint, that combined with unexpected cache eviction behavior caused higher memory churn, which made kernel scheduling slower on the GPU nodes; result was longer per-token latencies and increased timeouts upstream
[01:12] Tom Reynolds: just to clarify, are you saying the model variant itself was slower or that the cache interactions were the problem?
[01:20] Marcus Liu: good question — the quantized variant on its own matched perf in isolated bench tests, but under production concurrent workload the KV cache had unusual thrash because the variant's tokenization pattern led to less prefix reuse; so synergy between model variant and cache eviction policy is the likely root cause not a pure model regression
[01:38] Daniel Mercer: we also saw autoscaler behavior that didn't add nodes fast enough, I pulled the HPA logs and there was a delay in pod provisioning of ~90s, which made the tail worse
[01:50] Marcus Liu: yes our autoscaler config was using a smoothing window that assumed linear growth; combined with rapid fanout it underreacted. During the critical window we recommended rollback to stable variant and we pushed temporary dedicated capacity which mitigated the worst of it
[02:06] Priya Nair: the rollback helped, error rate dropped back to baseline in about 4 minutes but that spike cost us customer incidents, so we're trying to understand how to prevent recurrence and what SLA guardrails we need
[02:18] Sofia Patel: totally, the temporary Dedicated buffer we spun up was meant as a stopgap — Marcus, can you outline the permanent changes we recommend?
[02:28] Marcus Liu: sure — three prongs: 1) autoscaler retuning: shorten smoothing window, add proactive scale-up signal based on upstream fanout metrics; 2) KV-cache tuning: adjust eviction thresholds and increase cache capacity for the specific model family when quantized variants are used; 3) rollout controls: require canary traffic shaping (1-5% ramp) per model variant and an automated rollback trigger on p99 latency regression
[03:00] Daniel Mercer: for point 3, can Redwood enforce canary traffic on our hosted endpoints? we want those safety checks without manual steps
[03:07] Marcus Liu: yes, we can enforce rollout policies at the routing layer — we offer canary lane routing and automatic fallback to pinned stable variants, we just need an agreed config in the model descriptor and an API toggle; we'll provide a sample policy
[03:20] Priya Nair: about KV cache — can you share exact metrics that showed eviction thrash? our internal metrics don't map 1:1 with Redwood's instrumentation so we need aligned time-series
[03:30] Marcus Liu: absolutely, we'll export annotated traces and the cache hit/miss histograms keyed by model variant and timestamp; expect that to show the correlation, not just causation
[03:40] Tom Reynolds: any thoughts on a longer-term architecture change? we've talked about Dedicated vs self-hosting — is Dedicated effectively the safe middle ground?
[03:50] Sofia Patel: yes Dedicated gives predictable capacity and isolation which helps with noisy-neighbor issues; it also simplifies debugging because you have reserved nodes, but it's not a panacea — you still need rollout controls and cache tuning
[04:04] Daniel Mercer: cost will matter; we need numbers for a 3-month buffer and for a 12-month commit — can you send that?
[04:12] Sofia Patel: yes i'll send a short pricing options doc after the call, including temporary burst capacity pricing and an annual discounted commit for Dedicated
[04:20] Marcus Liu: another immediate mitigation — enable a temporary throttling layer on canary/experimental routes so a misbehaving model doesn't blast the cache; that buys time while autoscaler kicks in
[04:32] Priya Nair: good idea, we can add rate limits per route behind our aggregator service
[04:36] Lena Ortiz: from a CSM perspective we'll also update the post-incident runbook and include a checklist: collect traces, identify model variant, check KV cache metrics, confirm rollback, and open SE/CSM coordination page
[04:50] Daniel Mercer: what about observability retention? we had only 48h of fine-grain traces and that made early diagnosis harder
[04:58] Marcus Liu: we can extend retention for traces for a short window — Redwood offers a 30/90 day option as an add-on, we'll include that in Sofia's follow-up pricing note
[05:10] Tom Reynolds: curious — did you see any wide security implications or PII exposure during the incident?
[05:16] Sofia Patel: no evidence of data leakage, error types were runtime timeouts and model execution OOMs, we did verify audit logs and there were no abnormal access events
[05:25] Priya Nair: ok thanks, that's good to hear
[05:28] Marcus Liu: next technical items — we'll run an e2e staging replay using captured traffic with 2x fanout, and we'll instrument cache metrics per-variant. I'll share the exact repro steps so Argosy can run locally too
[05:42] Daniel Mercer: timeline for that?
[05:44] Marcus Liu: aiming week of 11/29, need you to approve a timeslot and provide the production traffic sample by 11/21
[05:52] Sofia Patel: quick recap of assigned owners and due dates — Marcus will send traces by 11/22, Priya will provide traffic sample 11/21, Sofia will send pricing 11/22, Lena will share runbook 11/25 — is that correct?
[06:08] Priya Nair: yes that's fine
[06:10] Tom Reynolds: once tests pass we'll consider a Dedicated buffer for peak hours and then revisit a longer commit after 30 days of stability
[06:20] Lena Ortiz: i'll schedule the follow-up review for 2 weeks after the test results, target 12/06, i'll include a short agenda
[06:28] Sofia Patel: thank you all, appreciate the partnership, we'll follow up quickly and keep Argosy in the loop, any final Qs?
[06:36] Daniel Mercer: no, thank you
[06:40] Tom Reynolds: thanks everyone
[06:42] Sofia Patel: meeting adjourned

Notes on transcription: some words may be mis-heard (e.g., kernel vs canal) and timestamps are approximate; recorded audio had brief crosstalk during the first 3 minutes.
